readingLines: Three things came out of your bag and stayed out. That is the decision, made at the door, in about four seconds. A feather on the plate, drawn once. Lightness is not innocence. It is a shorter list.

A feather, one line, no weight to it at all. You left something behind on purpose this week. The relief was immediate and slightly suspicious. Beginnings are subtraction. Most people expect the opposite and pack accordingly.
You are standing at the door with a lighter bag than you planned. The taxi does not check. The zip closed on the first try. That is the only test this card runs. A feather, once, in ink.
questions: What did you leave out?
Where did the relief come from?
Which three would you leave out?
meanings.libraryEntry: Packing is subtraction, and the decision happens at the door, in the four seconds when three things come out of the bag and stay out. That is the whole of it. Beginnings get imagined as accumulation, as gathering what you need, and in practice the moment anything actually starts is the moment a list gets shorter. A feather is one line on a plate with no weight in it, which is a hard thing to draw and an easy thing to carry. What tends to follow the subtraction is a relief so immediate that it feels like a mistake, and then a slow week of discovering that not one of the removed items was wanted. Nothing at the door is being inspected. The zip closing first time is the only test available, and it is a better test than the list was.

readingLines: You went with the short list and missed nothing. Not one of the things you left behind was needed. That is the ordinary result and it stays surprising. The bag was right. You were carrying an old estimate.

The bag is packed for four scenarios and the trip has one destination. You have repacked it twice. Preparation past a point is another word for reluctance. Every item has a reason. The reasons are not the problem.
You left too much behind and stood on a platform without a coat. Lightness has a floor and you found it by going through it. One cold morning. The list is a draft and not a principle.
questions: What did you not need?
How many scenarios are in there?
Whose list was that?
reversed.libraryEntry: Two ways the short list goes wrong, and one way it goes right. Right is unremarkable. You travel light, need none of what you left, and register mild surprise at an outcome that repeats every time, because the estimate in your head was built for a version of you from some years ago. The first failure is the bag packed for four scenarios when the trip has one destination. Every item in it can be justified, individually, and that is precisely the trouble, since preparation past a certain point is a different word for reluctance. The second failure is the platform in February with no coat. There is a floor under all this, and it gets located by dropping through it, which costs one cold morning and settles the question for years. The list is a draft. Treating it as a principle is how both failures start.

meanings.altText: A single feather drawn in one line, centered on the plate above the numeral.

readingLines: Every tool you need is on the bench and has been for three weeks. Nothing is missing. A flask on the plate, clean, empty, ready. The missing tool is starting. It is not on the bench because it is not a tool.

A flask, drawn plainly, with a measure line and nothing in it. You have the materials, the skill and the afternoon. Readiness is not a stage. It is a place people stop. Comfortably, and with everything arranged.
You arranged it all again on Sunday. Arranging is real work. It is also the most convincing way to not begin. The bench has been ready longer than the project has existed. One pour would settle it.
questions: What is already on your bench?
Where did you stop?
When was the bench last used?
meanings.libraryEntry: Everything required is already laid out on the bench, and was laid out a fortnight before that. That is the situation, and the useful part of it is that nothing is missing, which removes the most popular excuse in one stroke. The tool that is absent is starting, and starting cannot be laid out with the others. A flask on a plate is clean and empty and reads as ready, and a flask stays clean precisely by never being used. What makes this hard is that arranging is genuine work. It takes skill, it produces a visible result, it is pleasant, and it can be repeated indefinitely on Sunday afternoons without the project advancing by a single hour. Readiness is not a stage of anything. It is somewhere people stop, and the stopping is comfortable, and your bench looks like evidence of the opposite.

readingLines: You started it on Tuesday, badly, and the bench got messy inside ten minutes. That mess is the difference between this card upright and reversed. Nothing was ready. Everything was available. That is a lower bar and the only real one.

Your bench is arranged and photographed and the project is three months old. Preparation has become the project. That happens to most people and gets called being organised. A flask stays clean by not being used.
You bought a fourth tool this month for a job that needed none of the first three. Acquisition feels adjacent to progress and reliably is not. The bench is fuller. The afternoon is the same length.
questions: What did you start badly?
Which one is three months old?
What did the fourth tool add?
reversed.libraryEntry: One good outcome and two comfortable ones. The good one looks worse than the alternatives. It is a Tuesday, the thing gets going badly, and the bench is a mess inside ten minutes, and that mess is the entire distinction this card draws. Nothing was ready. Everything was to hand, which is a much lower bar and the only one that has ever mattered. The first comfortable outcome is preparation becoming the project, with the bench arranged, photographed, and three months older than the work. Almost everybody does this, and you have a Sunday version of it. The second is acquisition. A fourth tool arrives to serve a job the first three were already too many for, because buying feels adjacent to progress, and the bench is fuller afterwards, and the afternoon is exactly the length it was. Neither failure is laziness, which is what makes both of them so durable.

meanings.altText: A glass flask with one measure line, empty, drawn in line above the numeral.

readingLines: You answered it in the shower on Tuesday. Since then you asked four people. None of them told you anything you did not have at seven that morning. A crescent on the plate, half of it dark.

Second opinions have a function and it is rarely information. A crescent moon, one edge lit. What you collect after deciding is permission. It gets gathered from people who cannot know the details. The shower had all of them.

A crescent, half lit, half not, and the dark half is not empty. You know something you have not written down. It has been steady for a fortnight. Unwritten knowledge counts. It does not come with a receipt.
questions: What did you already answer?
Whose permission are you collecting?
Where were you when you knew?
meanings.libraryEntry: The answer arrived in the shower on Tuesday morning at about seven. Everything since then has been consultation, four people deep, and not one of those conversations added a fact that was unavailable in the bathroom. This is not a criticism of asking. It is a description of what asking after the fact is for, which is permission rather than information, and permission has to be sought from people who by definition cannot know the details of your life. A crescent shows one lit edge, and there is something in the unlit part. Knowledge that has never been written down still counts, and it comes with nothing you can show anybody, which is why it feels weaker than the fourth opinion and generally is not. The search for agreement has a known ending. It stops when one person agrees. The fifth conversation is available and would add nothing.

readingLines: You stopped asking on Thursday and went with the shower answer. It was right, or at least it was yours. Those two are closer together than the fourth opinion suggested. The fifth opinion was never collected. One decision, no committee.
You have four opinions and a decision you made before any of them arrived. Consultation after the fact is not research and never was. It is a search for one person to agree. It runs until one agrees.

The dark half has gone flat and you cannot hear anything from it. That happens. It is usually noise rather than absence. A crescent with no lit edge is still a moon. Nothing has to be known this week.
questions: When did you stop asking?
Which one agreed with you?
What is the noise?
reversed.libraryEntry: Three states, and the first is the one worth having. Asking stops, the shower answer gets used, and it turns out to be right, or at least to be yours, and being right and being yours are nearer neighbours than the fourth opinion allowed. No committee was convened. The second state is consultation running after a decision that was already made, which has never been research of any kind, and which continues until one person agrees, at which point it ends abruptly and gets called consensus. The third is the flat spell. The dark half stops speaking, nothing surfaces, and a silent stretch is far more often static than emptiness, and an unlit crescent is still a moon on the plate. Nothing needs to be known this week. That is a permission. It is also the only week in three that has asked nothing of you.

meanings.altText: A crescent moon drawn in line, one edge dark, centered above the plate numeral.

readingLines: Soup came out of a fridge you thought was empty. Three things past their best and one onion. A wheat sheaf on the plate, bound once. Plenty is a skill you have. It is not a delivery you received.

What reads as plenty here is competence, not weather. You fed people this week out of what was already there. The part worth noticing is that you did not go shopping. A sheaf, bound. Nothing arrived, it was assembled.

You have more to work with than the shelf suggests. That is a claim about your hands rather than your cupboard. A wheat sheaf, bound once. Drawn without ornament. The soup was good and it cost four pounds.
questions: What did you make from nearly nothing?
Who did you feed?
Where is your plenty actually kept?
meanings.libraryEntry: Soup gets made from a fridge that looked empty an hour earlier. Three things past their best, one onion, some stock. That is the card, and the reason it matters is that plenty in this deck is a skill rather than a windfall. Nothing arrived. It was assembled, by a person who could see four ingredients where the fridge appeared to hold none, and that seeing is the whole competence. A wheat sheaf is bound once and drawn without ornament, because the harvest is not the point and the binding is. What tends to go unremarked is exactly what makes it work. Provision done well conceals its own sums, so the table experiences plenty and never meets the constraint, and you get read as generous rather than as extremely good at this. Both are true. Only one is a skill.

readingLines: You made it from the fridge again and the constraint went unmentioned. All week. That invisibility is the compliment and also the cost. Good provision hides its own arithmetic. One of them thought you had planned it.

The fridge is genuinely empty and you have been making soup out of it anyway. Resourcefulness has a floor. Pretending otherwise is expensive. A sheaf can be bound thin. This one has been thin for months.

You cooked for nine people and ate standing up at the counter. Nine bowls out. Eight delivered. Provision that never turns inward is a habit rather than a virtue. There is a ninth bowl and your name is on it.
questions: Who thinks you planned it?
When did the shelf actually run out?
Where did you eat?
reversed.libraryEntry: Three states, and two of them cost the cook. The first is the ordinary triumph. Soup out of the fridge again, the constraint unmentioned, and one person at the table assuming it was planned, which is what competence of this kind always looks like from a chair. The second is the empty shelf. Resourcefulness has a floor. A binding can be drawn tight around very little, and months of that is information rather than a character test. Pretending otherwise gets expensive in ways that take a while to show. The third is the ninth bowl. Nine went out, eight were delivered, and the cook ate standing at the counter, because care that only ever points outward is a habit and not a virtue. The ninth bowl exists. Your name is on it. Whoever counts the bowls is the person who cooked.

meanings.altText: A bound sheaf of wheat drawn in line, centered on the plate above the numeral.

readingLines: Everyone mocks the two-signature rule and everyone uses it. You mocked it too. A standing stone on the plate, upright, unornamented. Structure gets its reputation from the people it inconveniences. It gets its value from the week it stops something.

A standing stone, one line, no decoration and no explanation. You kept to something boring this week that you could have skipped. It held. Rules that only prove themselves in the exception are impossible to defend on the other fifty weeks.

You are the one who follows the procedure. That gets you mocked in the good weeks and consulted in the bad ones. Both happen. A standing stone does nothing visible for years. Then a fence line runs off it.
questions: Which rule did you mock this week?
What did you keep to?
Who consults you in a bad week?
meanings.libraryEntry: There is a rule at work that everyone mocks and everyone uses. Two signatures, a form, a waiting period, something with no defenders and no exceptions. That rule is this card. Structure is judged by whoever it holds up, which is everybody, including you, weekly, and it earns its value from the single week it stops something expensive, which is invisible by design, because a prevented disaster leaves no evidence behind. A standing stone sits inert for a century and then a boundary gets surveyed from it. What makes this hard to argue about is the asymmetry. The cost of the rule is felt fifty times a year by named people, and the benefit is felt once by nobody in particular. Being the person who keeps to it means mockery in the good weeks and consultation in the bad ones, and both of those are the job.

readingLines: The boring rule stopped something expensive on Thursday and you were the reason it was still in place. No thanks arrived. That is standard. Structure is thanked at a rate of roughly zero and relied on continuously. It held anyway.

The rule has outlived the problem it was written for and you are still enforcing it. Structure with no live purpose is furniture. A standing stone in the middle of a field gets ploughed around for a century. The reason went unrecorded.

You made a rule at four in the afternoon to settle an argument. It has been load-bearing ever since. That was never planned. Structure invented in irritation outlasts structure invented on purpose. Yours is holding something up.
questions: What did the rule stop?
Which rule outlived its reason?
What is your rule holding up?
reversed.libraryEntry: Three states of the boring rule. In the first it works and receives nothing for it. Something expensive gets stopped on a Thursday, no thanks arrive, and structure continues being relied on at a gratitude rate of roughly zero, which is the normal operating condition rather than a grievance. In the second the problem it was drafted against has been gone for years. A rule with no live purpose is furniture, and a stone left in a field gets worked around for generations by people who were never told what it marks. The third is the accidental one. A rule improvised late one afternoon to end an argument turns out to be load-bearing, which nobody planned and nobody reviews. Rules made in a bad mood outlast rules made in a meeting. That is worth knowing about the rules you made yourself.

meanings.altText: A single upright standing stone drawn in line, centered above the plate numeral.

readingLines: You do Sunday the way it was done in the house you grew up in. The roast, the timing, the argument at four. A skep on the plate, one shape, repeated. You never chose any of it. Most of it is fine.

Inherited practice is not belief. It does most of belief's work. A beehive skep, drawn once, the same shape for four hundred years. You kept a form this week without examining it. Forms hold weight either way.

A skep, one shape, no innovation anywhere in it. Something in your week runs on a pattern older than your opinion of it. That is not hypocrisy. Most of what holds a family together was never put to a vote.
questions: Which part did you choose?
Where did that form come from?
What runs without a vote?
meanings.libraryEntry: Sunday runs on the pattern of a house you have not lived in for twenty years. A roast at a fixed hour, a fixed order of events, a disagreement mid-afternoon. None of it was chosen, and the striking thing is how little that matters, because inherited practice does most of the work belief does and asks for none of the commitment. A beehive skep has been one shape for centuries and functions without anybody holding a theory of bees. Where this gets uncomfortable is the gap between doing a thing and endorsing it. That gap is normal, it is not hypocrisy, and very little of what keeps a family in one piece was ever voted on, or would survive being. The live question here is narrow. Not whether the form is justified, but whether it still fits the people currently at the table.

readingLines: You kept the Sunday and dropped the argument at four o'clock. One change, deliberate, inside a form you left standing. That is the whole edit. Tradition survives editing better than inspection. The roast was unchanged and the afternoon was not.

You looked at the whole arrangement and could not say why any of it is done. That is an honest position. It does not require dismantling anything. A skep works without a theory of bees. Nor does Sunday.

You are running a Sunday that suits none of the people at the table. Inherited forms have an expiry. They do not announce it. Four people, one pattern, no one consulted. The house it fitted is not this house.
questions: What did you drop?
Who set the four o'clock?
Whose Sunday is it now?
reversed.libraryEntry: Three positions, and the middle one is more comfortable than it sounds. The first is the edit. The Sunday stays, the four o'clock argument goes, one deliberate change inside a form left otherwise standing, because tradition survives editing considerably better than it survives inspection. The second is honest ignorance. You survey the arrangement and can account for none of it, which is a defensible place to stand and obliges you to dismantle nothing, since nobody keeping bees in a skep ever required an account of bees, and Sunday asks even less. The third is the form that outlived its household. Four people, one pattern, none of them consulted, and inherited forms carry an expiry they never announce. The house it fitted was a different house. That is a fact about that house and not about the people in this one. One of those three is where your Sunday currently sits.

meanings.altText: A woven beehive skep drawn in line, centered on the plate above the numeral.

keywords: a yes that cannot be walked back
readingLines: Sending it changes two lives. Not sending it changes one. Your reply has been in drafts for four days. Both of those facts have been true the whole time. Two entwined stems, and no way to unwind them afterwards.

Two stems, grown together, neither able to be pulled out cleanly. A yes of this kind cannot be walked back. You already know that. That is why it is still in drafts. Four days is accuracy about the stakes rather than indecision.

You have written it and you have not sent it. The gap between those is where you live this week. Reversible choices deserve speed. This one is not reversible. The four days are the correct price of that difference.
questions: What is sitting in your drafts?
Who else does it change?
When does the draft go?
meanings.libraryEntry: A reply that would change two lives has been sitting in your drafts for four days. Nine words, already written, not sent. What makes this card difficult has nothing to do with romance, which is where it usually gets filed. It is about a yes that cannot be walked back. Most choices are reversible, and the correct speed for a reversible choice is fast, because the cost of being wrong is one correction. This is the other kind. Two stems grown together do not come apart cleanly, and the four days in drafts are not indecision. They are an accurate reading of the stakes, taken by someone who knows the difference between the two categories and is behaving correctly in the second. Nothing here says send it. What it says is that the delay is proportionate, and that declining to send is a choice too, and it gets made again every morning.

readingLines: You sent it. The reply took nine words to write and four days to allow. Whatever happens next, the version of you that could not send it is finished. That ending happened the moment the message left. Two lives moved.

Your draft is still there and it is now three weeks old. Not sending is also a decision. It is being made daily, in small instalments. That is the only way this decision ever gets made. Nothing has been avoided.

You sent something you could walk back. Then called it the big one. Hedged yeses are common. They are not the same instrument. Two stems can be laid next to each other without growing together. That arrangement is comfortable, reversible, and not this card.
questions: What ended when you sent it?
Where is the draft now?
Which yes did you actually send?
reversed.libraryEntry: Sent, unsent, and hedged. In the first the message leaves, and whatever follows, whoever you were while it sat unsent is gone, and that ending happened at the moment of sending rather than in whatever the answer turns out to be. Two lives moved and one of them was yours. In the second the draft is three weeks old, and the refusal is renewed each morning in small amounts, which is how this particular decision always gets made, and nothing at all has been avoided. Both of those are recognisable and neither is a failure. The third is the hedge. Something walk-back-able gets sent while being labelled the real thing, and stems laid side by side without growing together are comfortable and reversible and not what this card is about. The hedge answers a different question than the one asked.

meanings.altText: Two stems grown together, entwined in line drawing, centered above the plate numeral.

readingLines: Speed you chose feels like control. Speed that chose you feels identical from inside the same car. A spoked wheel on the plate, turning. Both hands are on it. Only one of those two is driving.

A spoked wheel, drawn true, no blur on it. You went fast this week and you meant to. Momentum you generated behaves differently from momentum you are inside of. The tell is simple. Stopping is either available or it is not.
You have both hands on the wheel and you are enjoying it. That is allowed. It is the whole card. Directed speed is a real achievement. It looks exactly like the other kind from the passenger seat.
questions: Chosen, or arrived?
Where could you stop?
Who is in the passenger seat?
meanings.libraryEntry: Driving fast with both hands on the wheel is one of two situations, and they are indistinguishable from inside the car. In the first, the speed was chosen, generated, and is being directed by whoever is steering. In the second, the speed arrived from elsewhere and the person at the wheel is steering something already in motion. Both feel like competence, both look like competence from the passenger seat, and the difference matters enormously. A spoked wheel drawn true has no blur on it and gives no indication of which case applies. There is one reliable tell, and it is not how fast the thing is moving. It is whether stopping is available, a question answerable in about four seconds and very rarely asked while the road is clear and the driving is going well. You were driving this week, and the tell is available to you in about four seconds.

readingLines: You slowed at a junction you could have taken at speed, and nothing required it. That is the test. It does not come up often. A wheel that can stop is a wheel. The rest is a hill.

The car is going fast and you are holding the wheel of something you did not start. That is a common arrangement. It is not a failure of nerve. Steering is available and braking is a separate question.
You have stopped and the car is stationary and you are still holding the wheel. Readiness to move is not movement. A spoked wheel at rest is a circle. Six weeks is a long time in a lay-by.
questions: When did you last slow down?
What can you actually steer?
How long in the lay-by?
reversed.libraryEntry: Three positions, and the first is the only one that settles anything. A junction that could have been taken at speed gets taken slowly instead, with nothing requiring it. That is the examination, it is set rarely, and the capacity to stop is what distinguishes a wheel from a slope. The second is steering a thing that was already moving before you arrived, which is an ordinary arrangement and not a failure of nerve, and in it steering is genuinely available while braking is a separate question with a different answer. The third is the lay-by. Stopped, stationary, hands still on the wheel, because readiness to move is a comfortable state that resembles movement from the driver's seat and from nowhere else. At rest the whole apparatus is just a circle, and six weeks of it is a long while. The junction is the only one of the three that answers anything.

meanings.altText: A spoked cart wheel drawn in line, centered on the plate above the numeral.

keywords: the floor at the edge of the bed
readingLines: You are on the floor at the edge of the bed. The cat has not come out. Force has never once worked here. Not once, in the entire history of frightened animals. Strength here is the patience to stay on the floor.
A small perched bird, no cage anywhere near it. Whatever you were gentle with this week did not respond to being pushed. You knew that before you tried. Gentleness is the technique and not the mood.

You held your temper with something that deserved it. That is the whole card. It is more expensive than it sounds. Force is faster and it does not work on frightened things. Staying on the floor is what took the strength.
questions: Who are you waiting for?
What did you not push?
Where did you hold it?
meanings.libraryEntry: A person is flat on the carpet beside a bed, talking quietly to an animal that has stayed under it. That is the picture, and everything this card has to say is inside it. Force is faster, and force has never once worked on a frightened creature, and the person on the floor knows this from experience rather than from principle. What it costs is the hour. You spent one like that recently. Gentleness of this kind is not a temperament and not a mood, and it is not niceness. It is a technique with a known duration, applied by someone who would very much prefer to be doing something else. The cat comes out eventually, on its own schedule, usually once the room has stopped watching, and the last quiet hour gets no credit for that while being the reason it happened. Strength is the wrong word for it and the only one available.

readingLines: The cat came out on its own at eleven, when you had stopped looking at it. Nothing you did in the last hour caused that. Everything you did in the first hour made it possible. Both are true.

You reached under the bed and got scratched. Force applied to a frightened animal produces exactly one result. It is on your hand. Not cruelty. Impatience, which is far more common and leaves the same mark.

Six weeks on this floor. The cat is comfortable under there now. Patience with no limit stops being patience. Waiting can become the thing you do instead of deciding. Gentleness has a version that never asks for anything.
questions: When did it come out?
What were you out of?
How long have you been waiting?
reversed.libraryEntry: Two failures and one success, and the success is the least visible of the three. The success is the animal coming out at eleven, by itself, once the watching stopped, with nothing in the final hour causing it and everything in your first hour making it possible. Both of those are true and only one of them feels like a result. The first failure is the hand under the bed. Force applied to a frightened creature produces a single outcome and it is a scratch, and the cause is almost never cruelty. It is haste, which is commoner by far and marks a hand identically. The second failure is the floor becoming a residence. Endless patience is no longer patience, waiting stands in for deciding very comfortably, and there is a form of gentleness that never asks anybody for anything and calls that a virtue.

meanings.altText: A small bird perched on a bare twig, drawn in line above the plate numeral.

keywords: what surfaces when the feed stops
readingLines: You left the phone in the kitchen for one evening. By nine you had an opinion you did not know you held. A lantern on the plate. Small light, short range. That is the whole method, and it is unglamorous.

A lantern, one flame, lighting about four feet of path. Solitude at this scale is not a retreat. It is an evening. What surfaced when your feed stopped had been there all week. It was underneath other people's sentences.
Opinions form in the gaps and the gaps have been sold off. A lantern lights four feet. That is enough to walk by and not enough to survey with. You had one evening of it this week. Something arrived.
questions: What surfaced by nine?
Whose sentences were on top?
Where are your gaps?
meanings.libraryEntry: One evening, phone in another room, and by about nine an opinion surfaces that you did not know you were holding. That is the entire content of this card, and its smallness is the point. A lantern lights roughly four feet of path, which is enough for walking and no use at all for surveying, and a lantern has never been mistaken for a floodlight except in retrospect. What makes the evening productive is not depth. It is the absence of other people's sentences, which are the raw material of most of what passes for your own view, and which arrive continuously and free. Whatever came up had been sitting under them all week. The yield is usually one small decision and a mildly dull evening. Boring is the correct texture. Anything more dramatic came from somewhere else. One evening is the entire method and there is no larger version available.

readingLines: Your phone stayed in the kitchen and the evening was long and slightly boring. Boring is the correct texture. Nothing profound happened. One small thing got decided, which is the usual yield and worth the evening.

You took the whole evening and spent it reading about other people's evenings. Solitude with a feed in it is not solitude. That is a common substitution and it does not feel like one. The lantern was lit. It was pointed at a screen.

The phone has been in the other room for three months. You have stopped telling people things. Withdrawal and solitude use identical equipment. One lantern, one room, one person. The difference is only visible from in there.
questions: What got decided?
Which evenings were you reading about?
Who have you not told?
reversed.libraryEntry: Three uses of one evening. In the first it works and looks like nothing. The phone stays in the kitchen, the hours are long and mildly dull, one small thing gets decided, and that is the standard yield rather than a disappointment. In the second the evening gets taken and then spent reading about other people's evenings, which is a common substitution and does not feel like one from inside it. The flame was lit all evening. It faced a screen the whole time. The third is the long version. Three months of the phone in the other room, and a person who has stopped telling anybody anything, because withdrawal and solitude run on identical equipment and are told apart only from inside the room. The equipment is identical down to the room. What separates the two is whether anything comes back out of it. Your answer to that is the only one that counts.

meanings.altText: A small lantern with one flame drawn in line, centered above the plate numeral.

readingLines: Six good weeks ended on a Tuesday and no explanation arrived. That is how weather ends. An ammonite spiral, tightening inward, the same curve all the way down. The run was real. Your account of why was the invention.

An ammonite spiral, chamber after chamber. Same shape, different size each time. Something good ran for a while and then stopped. You were not the cause of either end of it. That is worse news going up than coming down.
You had a good run and then you did not. Both halves were weather. The mistake in the middle was the story where you had worked out how to keep it going. Everyone writes that story, every time.
questions: What did you take credit for?
Which part was yours?
Where did the story come from?
meanings.libraryEntry: A run of six good weeks ends on a Tuesday, without explanation, the way weather ends. The run was real and the ending is real, and the part that was invented is the middle, where a story got written in which the run was being caused by something you had worked out. Everyone writes that story. It is nearly irresistible, and it is harder to hear on the way up than on the way down, because up is where it feels like insight. An ammonite adds chamber after chamber in the same curve at increasing size, and the shell holds no view about which chamber it is in. What this card declines to offer is a prediction. It says the run happened, that the ending has no message in it, and that the authorship you assigned yourself was the only unreliable part of the sequence. The weather is not about you. That is the good news in it.

readingLines: The run ended and you did not take it personally. That is unusual and worth recording. Weather that stops is not a verdict on the person standing under it. You appear to have known that on the day.

The run is still going and you have an explanation for it. Everyone does at this point in the spiral. An account of why the weather is good is the most confident writing anyone produces. It dates badly.

Eight weeks of a bad stretch. You have built a theory about yourself out of it. Downturns produce the same false authorship as good runs. The direction changes and the error does not. A spiral has no opinion about which chamber you are in.
questions: Who did you not blame?
What is your explanation?
Whose theory is that?
reversed.libraryEntry: Three readings of the same spiral. The first is the rare one. The run ends and it does not get taken personally, because a stretch that ends passes no judgement on whoever stood under it, and knowing that on the day rather than six months later is unusual enough to write down. The second is the confident stretch. The run is still going, an explanation for it exists, and a theory explaining a good stretch is the most assured writing anybody does and the fastest to date badly. The third runs the same error in reverse. Two bad months, and a theory about yourself built out of them, because downturns manufacture false authorship exactly as reliably as good runs do. The direction changes and the mistake does not. A shell adds chambers in one curve and has no opinion about which one you are in.

meanings.altText: A coiled ammonite spiral drawn in line, tightening inward, above the plate numeral.

readingLines: One column says what it cost. The other says what it paid. Same ink, same hand, same page. You read only one of them this week. A balance scale on the plate, level, holding both columns at once.

A balance scale, level, both pans loaded. Fairness is not a feeling. It is not a mood you arrive at. It is two columns written in the same ink by the same person. You did the honest version of this recently, on something specific.

You gave something a fair reading this week. Including the unflattering parts. That is rarer than being right. A scale reads level only when both pans are loaded honestly. The second pan is the one that gets left light.
questions: Which column did you skip?
What did it actually pay?
Whose account are you keeping?
meanings.libraryEntry: Two columns, one page, the same ink in both. What it cost on the left and what it paid on the right, written by the same hand, at the same sitting, with the same care. That is the whole instrument, and almost everyone runs it half-loaded, because one column is easy to fill and the other is the one that makes the total inconvenient. Which column gets shortchanged varies by person and stays consistent within a person. A balance scale reads level for a reason, and the reason is arithmetic rather than virtue. Fairness in this card has nothing to do with feeling fair, and feeling fair is a poor indicator, since a page with one pan light also comes to a total and the total looks just as tidy. What is asked here is narrow. One decision, both columns, same ink, and then keeping the answer even when it goes against you.

readingLines: You added up both columns and the answer was not the one you wanted. Then you kept it. Holding an honest total that goes against you is the entire content of this card. It takes about a day to stop stinging.

One column is in ink and the other is in pencil. That is the ordinary way this gets done. It is not lying. The costs are precise and the payments approximate, or the reverse. Either way your scale reads level on a page that is not.

Every account gets settled in your head at eleven at night. Fairness turned inward without limit is not justice. It is a tribunal. This scale weighs one decision at a time. It does not weigh a whole person.
questions: What total did you keep?
Which column is in pencil?
When does the weighing stop?
reversed.libraryEntry: The honest version and the two dishonest ones, and the dishonest pair are not lies. In the honest version both columns get added, the answer comes out against you, and you keep it anyway, which stings for roughly a day and then stops. That is the entire achievement. In the first failure one side is inked and the other pencilled. Costs precise and payments approximate, or the reverse, and the pans still balance above a page that does not, and nobody involved has said anything untrue. The second failure is scale creep. Every account settled nightly, in the head, at eleven, with fairness turned all the way inward and no stopping condition, which is a tribunal rather than a justice. The instrument takes one decision at a time. Handing it a whole person is a category error, and it produces a number every time.

meanings.altText: A two-pan balance scale hanging level, drawn in line above the plate numeral.

readingLines: Your train is ninety minutes late and there is nothing to do about it. You did not choose this hour and would never have scheduled it. A chrysalis on the plate, hanging, doing invisible work. The hour counts anyway.

A chrysalis, suspended and sealed. It is doing something you cannot watch. Waiting looks identical to nothing from outside. Your week put you somewhere you did not pick. Time you did not budget. You have already thought something you would not have thought.

Chosen stillness is a practice. Imposed stillness is a platform at Crewe with a coffee going cold. The second one produces more, more often. That is annoying and well documented. You would not have given yourself that hour.
questions: What did the delay hand you?
What surfaced in the extra hour?
When did you last stop on purpose?
meanings.libraryEntry: The train is ninety minutes late, the platform is cold, and there is nothing available to do about any of it. That is the situation this card describes, and the useful thing about it is that you would never have scheduled it. An hour given to yourself on purpose is a practice, and practices are good, and they are also rare and easily postponed. An hour taken from you by a signalling fault arrives whether or not you had planned on it. What tends to happen in that hour is small and hard to report. A thought surfaces that had been queued behind the ordinary noise, and it is usually about something you already knew. A chrysalis does its work sealed and unwatched and looks from outside like a thing hanging on a twig. You cannot photograph the middle of this. You can notice, afterwards, that it happened.

readingLines: The delay handed you an hour and you used it. Ninety minutes. Using it looked like sitting still and staring at a departure board. That is what use looks like here. Nothing got produced and something got noticed.

You filled the ninety minutes with your phone and arrived with the same head you left with. That is the ordinary outcome and it is not a moral event. The hour was still handed to you. It went back unopened.

The stillness has stopped being imposed and become the arrangement. Hanging is a stage. Not an address. A chrysalis that never opens is not resting. A pause you were handed is not a pause you moved into. The difference is real.
questions: What did you notice at the station?
Where did the ninety minutes go?
Handed to you, or moved into?
reversed.libraryEntry: Two ways the handed hour goes, and one edge case worth naming. It gets used, which looks like nothing, since using it means sitting on a bench watching a departure board while a thought surfaces that had been queued behind the noise. Or it goes back unopened, filled with a phone, and you arrive with the head you left with, and that is the ordinary outcome rather than a moral event. Neither of those is a failure and both happen to everybody. The edge case is when the pause stops being imposed. Hanging is a stage rather than an address, and a chrysalis that does not open is not resting, and the difference between a pause you were handed and one you have moved into is real and only visible from inside. That distinction is the whole of the reversal. Everything else here is just a late train.

meanings.altText: A chrysalis hanging from a twig, drawn in line, centered above the plate numeral.

readingLines: You pulled the dead stems out. The bed is empty now. That emptiness is the work, finished. Something in your life ended this season and you were the one who cleared it. An empty bed in November is not a failed garden.

Something ended and you are standing in the space where it was. That space is wider than it looks in November. A bare teasel head. Seed gone, structure still standing. You are allowed to call it over on your own schedule.

Autumn does this to every bed in the country. Inside the same fortnight. Yours is not being singled out. The stems come out, the ground stays. The ground is the part that was always doing the work. You are still here.
questions: What did you clear this season?
Where are you standing now?
What is still in the ground?
meanings.libraryEntry: The dead stems come out in October and what is left is bare soil, and every year a gardener looks at that bed and reads it as failure. It is the opposite. The emptiness is the work, completed, on schedule, by a person who did the pulling. Something of yours ended this autumn. You may have ended it yourself, or watched it end, or spent three months knowing it was over before anything moved, and all three of those are endings and none of them is a mistake. What stays is the ground. Beds do not lose their soil when they lose their planting, and the part that was doing the work all along is still exactly where it was. This card names the difficulty and does not soften it. It also does not pretend the ground went anywhere. You are standing on it.

readingLines: You cleared it. You were sad about it. Both happened in the same week. That combination is the ordinary shape of an ending done properly. No contradiction there. The bed is empty and you are allowed to mind.

The stems are still standing in December and you know they are dead. Leaving them there is not denial. It is a way of not doing it yet. That is a different thing, and it costs something. The bed can wait.

You pulled everything, including two that were alive. Clearing at speed does not stop to check. That is what haste in autumn costs. It is a small loss inside a correct decision. The bed was still right.
questions: What are you allowed to mind?
When does the bed get cleared?
What went out with it?
reversed.libraryEntry: Two things happen to an autumn clearing and neither is a moral failing. Either it does not happen, or it happens too fast. Stems left standing into December are not denial. They are a method of postponement, which takes its own kind of effort, and the bed waits without penalty because beds do. Clearing at speed is the other one, and it pulls two live plants along with the twelve dead ones, because haste does not stop to check. Both of those sit inside a decision that was still correct. What the reversal is not is a verdict on your timing. Autumn reaches every bed in the country within a fortnight of every other and consults none of them, and the ground under yours held through all of it. You are allowed to have minded, and for longer than seemed reasonable.

meanings.altText: A bare teasel head drawn in line, centered on the plate above the numeral.

readingLines: Your eleventh version of the soup differs from the tenth by a quarter teaspoon. That is the whole method. It is extremely boring. Two vessels, joined by a stream. Nothing here arrives by a leap.

Two vessels joined by a moving stream, neither of them full. You changed one small thing this week. It was the right size of change. Small adjustments are unimpressive. They are also the only ones that hold. The good version is boringly near the last one.

You resisted the urge to fix it all at once. That urge is strong. It produces version one again, from scratch, with new mistakes. A quarter teaspoon is not a compromise. It is the resolution the problem actually has.
questions: What did you adjust by a quarter?
Which small thing did you change?
Where were you tempted to start over?
meanings.libraryEntry: The version that works differs from the previous version by a quarter teaspoon, and that is the least satisfying sentence in this deck. It is also how almost everything gets good. Two vessels with a stream between them, neither one full, the level moving slowly between them. What makes this hard is not the technique, which a child can follow. It is that increments produce no story. There is nothing to tell at a dinner table afterwards, no moment where the thing turned, and no version you can point to as the breakthrough, because there was not one. The competing urge is to throw the pot out and rebuild from scratch, which feels decisive and delivers version one with a fresh set of mistakes, several of which were already solved. Temperance is a very dull name for the discipline of changing one small thing and tasting it before changing another.

readingLines: Version eleven works and it tastes almost exactly like version ten. You cannot point to the change. The change is still why it works. Increments make a poor story and a reliable soup. The recipe never gets asked for.

You threw the whole pot out and started again from nothing. That happens. It is usually about frustration rather than about the recipe. Version one has a fresh set of mistakes in it. Some of them are the ones you already fixed.

You have adjusted eleven times now. The dish is not the problem. Increments are a way of moving. They are also a way of not moving. Eleven versions of nearly the same thing is a decision avoided. Carefully, and in a kitchen.
questions: What tastes right now?
What did you already fix once?
Adjusting, or avoiding?
reversed.libraryEntry: Two ways the method fails, and one of them looks like decisiveness. The clean case first. Version eleven works, tastes very nearly like the tenth, and you cannot trace it to any single change, and the untraceable change is precisely why it works, which is why nobody asks how it was done. The first failure is the fresh start. The whole pot goes out, the rebuild feels like action, and version one arrives with a new set of mistakes, some of them already solved two weeks ago, and the trigger is nearly always frustration rather than the dish. The second failure is subtler and more comfortable. Eleven quarter-teaspoon adjustments to a dish that was never the problem, because incrementing is a way of moving and also an excellent way of not moving, and both look identical from the stove. The taste is the only test that settles it.

meanings.altText: Two vessels joined by a moving stream, drawn in line above the plate numeral.

readingLines: You opened it again without deciding to. That is the whole mechanism and it is not a character flaw. A bramble knot, grown from a hundred separate evenings, none of which was the problem. The knot is still a knot.

A bramble knot, drawn in line. No beginning visible anywhere in it. None of this was chosen once. It was chosen on a hundred evenings, each of them harmless. The compound is what you are looking at. Brambles are not villains. They are very good at this.

You know exactly which app it is and how long the average evening runs. Naming it is not the same as being ashamed of it. A knot has ends. Finding one takes longer than pulling it. Pulling is the part most people start with.
questions: What opens without you deciding?
Which evening would you have skipped?
Where does the knot start?
meanings.libraryEntry: A bramble knot is not built on purpose. It arrives by accretion, from a hundred separate evenings, and not one of those evenings was the problem, which is exactly why the thing is hard to see and harder to date. You know which app it is. You could probably estimate the average evening to within ten minutes, and the estimate would be low, and none of that is a character defect. It is a compound of small permissions. Brambles are extremely good at this and hold no opinion about you at all. The useful fact about a knot is that it has ends. Locating an end takes longer than hauling on it, and pulling is where most attempts begin, which is why most attempts tighten it. This card does not tell you to cut anything. It says the knot grew the ordinary way, and that its main requirement is privacy.

readingLines: You put it in a drawer for one evening. The evening was long and fine. One evening is not a cure and was never offered as one. It was a demonstration. The knot loosened by exactly the amount you loosened it.

The knot is tighter than it was in spring. You stopped counting the evenings. Growth like this is silent and does not announce a threshold. A bramble does not decide to take a garden. It takes one by not being cut.

You call this a weakness. It has been getting stronger on that diet. Shame is not a cutting tool. It keeps the evenings private. Privacy is the one condition brambles actually need. A number said out loud to another person is no longer private.
questions: What did the long evening feel like?
When did you stop counting?
Who knows the number?
reversed.libraryEntry: Two states, and one of them is only visible from a distance. In the first, you put the thing in a drawer for a single evening and the evening turns out to be long and fine, and a single evening cures nothing and never claimed to. It is a demonstration that the loosening is available. In the second, the tangle has thickened since spring and the evenings stopped being counted some months ago, because growth of this kind is silent and never announces a threshold. What makes the second state persist is not weakness. It is privacy. Shame keeps the number unsaid, and unsaid is the one condition brambles require, so the shame and the bramble end up on the same side. A figure spoken to one other person has stopped being private. That is all this entry claims. It is also the only part of it that costs you anything.

meanings.altText: A tangled bramble knot drawn in line, centered on the plate above the numeral.

readingLines: You built it, you maintained it, and this week you watched it come down. All three of those are true at once, and none of them cancels the others. What you knew and couldn't say is now visible from the road. That part, at least, is over.

Something you built came down this week. It went fast at the end, after being slow for a long time, the way these things go. You're allowed to just stand here for a minute. The card stands with you. The ground under both of you held.

Trees fall in an afternoon after growing for forty years. The afternoon gets all the attention. The drying takes seasons and no one photographs that part. Only the clearing is visible from where you stand today, and it is honestly wide.
questions: What can you admit now?
What is still standing?
Where does the light reach now?
meanings.libraryEntry: Lightning takes a fraction of a second and the tree is on the ground by the end of the afternoon, and that afternoon gets all the attention, including yours. The forty years of growing get none. Neither does the clearing, which runs for seasons, in loads, with long gaps where nothing gets touched at all. Something you built came down. You built it, you maintained it, and you watched it fall, and all three of those are true at the same time without cancelling each other. That is the part that is hardest to hold. What you knew and could not say is visible from the road now. That much is over. The ground held through it, which is a plain fact about the ground rather than a consolation, and it happens to be the most useful fact available. Only the clearing is visible from where you stand today. It is honestly wide.

readingLines: The tree came down in April and you have been clearing since. The falling was the fast part. What takes the years is the drying and the hauling. Also the not thinking about it for whole weeks at a time. That is also progress.

The strike is old news. The clearing is done. The sky over that spot is now just the sky. Nothing about this is a return to before. You are standing in a different field. Level, and with more light in it than the old one had.

You are rebuilding on the same footprint and using the same measurements. That is allowed. It is worth knowing you are doing it. Some of the old plan was good. Some of it is why the tree was standing where the lightning went.
questions: What have you cleared already?
What grows there now?
Which measurements are you reusing?
reversed.libraryEntry: The falling is the short part. It photographs well and it is over in an afternoon, and everything afterwards is drying and hauling and long stretches of not thinking about it, which goes unrecorded as progress and which is exactly what progress looks like here. At some distance the strike becomes old news, the clearing finishes, and the sky above that gap is only sky, and the field that remains is not the old field restored. It is a different field, level, with more light in it. The one thing worth naming is the rebuild on the same footprint. Reusing your old measurements is permitted and common, and some of that old plan was good, and some of it is the reason the tree stood exactly where the lightning went. Both parts of that are true. Knowing which is which is a job for later, and later is allowed to be much later.

meanings.altText: A lightning-struck tree drawn in line, trunk split, centered above the plate numeral.

readingLines: A tap left barely on, running into a barrel all night. By morning there is four inches in it. A seven-pointed star on the plate. Refill is a schedule and not an event. You have been on one for a fortnight.

Recovery does not announce itself and it does not arrive. It accumulates at a rate you cannot feel hourly. A star of seven points, drawn small. You are better off than a fortnight ago. It did not feel like anything.
You have been sleeping slightly better and you noticed on Thursday. Slightly is the operative word. It is not a small one. A barrel fills from a tap you cannot hear. Four inches is four inches.
questions: What has been refilling slowly?
Where is your barrel now?
When did you notice?
meanings.libraryEntry: A tap left barely running into a rain barrel overnight puts four inches in it by morning, and at no point during those hours could anybody have watched it happening. That is the card. Recovery of any kind works on this schedule, which is to say it accumulates rather than arrives, and it does so at a rate below the threshold of hourly noticing. A seven-pointed star drawn small is the least dramatic emblem in the deck and the most accurate one here. What makes this hard to trust is the absence of an event. There is no turning point to name, no morning it changed, and nothing to point at as the cause, so the improvement gets credited to luck or dismissed as imagination. The level is the level. Four inches up is four inches up. Your barrel is four inches up or it is not, and either way the tap decides it.

readingLines: The barrel is fuller than it was and you can point to nothing that did it. That is how it works. No event and no turning point. The level is four inches up from a fortnight ago.

You are checking the barrel eight times a day and once at night. Watched refill is slower than unwatched refill. That is not physics and it is reliably true. The tap is on. Checking adds nothing to it.

Your tap has been off for a month and the level has not moved. That is worth stating plainly rather than gently. A dry barrel is not a slow one. Refill needs the tap open. That is a separate matter from patience.
questions: What is four inches up?
How often are you checking?
Whose tap is it?
reversed.libraryEntry: Three states of the barrel, and one of them is not slowness. The first is the working one. The level is up, nothing that caused it can be identified, and there was no event, no turning point, and no morning on which it changed, which is exactly how a refill schedule presents. The second is the watching. Eight checks a day and one at night, and watched refill runs slower than unwatched refill, which is not physics and holds up reliably anyway. The flow continues regardless. Observation contributes no water. The third needs saying plainly rather than gently. A month has passed with the tap shut and the level exactly where it was, and dryness is a different condition from slowness. A closed tap fills nothing however long it is waited on, and waiting is the wrong instrument for it. Only you can see which of the three you are in.

meanings.altText: A seven-pointed star drawn in line, centered on the plate above the numeral.

readingLines: At two in the morning it is enormous. At nine it is a phone call and nothing more. Same facts, both times. The difference is not information. Knowing that at nine does not help you at two.

A moon on the plate and a moth in front of it. You were awake at two. The shape of the thing was wrong. Not exaggerated. A different animal, using the same facts. It had your full attention because the rest of the world was shut.

You lost some sleep to something that is a manageable size in daylight. That is not a failure of perspective. Night has fewer objects in it. The one you have gets bigger. The moth is not wrong about the moon being the brightest thing.
questions: What is it at nine?
Which animal was it at two?
Where did the size come from?
meanings.libraryEntry: The same problem has a two in the morning version and a nine in the morning version, and the facts are identical in both. Only the size changes, and it changes enormously. None of that is a lapse of perspective, and a calmer person would not have dodged it either. Night has fewer objects in it than day, so whatever is in the room takes up all of it, and a moth in the dark is not wrong in judging the moon the brightest object available. What the card names is the gap, and it declines to tell you the daylight version is the true one. Both readings use real facts. The night version is simply working in a smaller room, and with more confidence than the room supports. The one genuine hazard here is deciding at that hour, since a decision taken at two gets taken again at nine.

readingLines: You waited until nine and made the call and it took four minutes. The two in the morning version does not have to be argued with. It has to be outlasted. You outlasted it by sleeping badly and then getting up.

It is three in the morning. Your problem has grown a face. Fear at this hour is not information about the problem. It is information about the hour. The face belongs to the hour. It was not there at four in the afternoon.

You have started making decisions at two in the morning. That is the hazard. The two in the morning version is confident. It is working from a smaller room. Decisions taken there get taken again at nine.
questions: How long did it actually take?
What did it look like at four?
What got decided at two?
reversed.libraryEntry: Two ways this goes and neither of them is a lapse. In the first, you lose the hours and then make the call at nine and it takes four minutes, and the night version was never something to argue with. It was something to outlast, and a bad night followed by getting up is how outlasting works. In the second, the hour is three and the thing has grown a face, and the fear at that hour is information about the hour rather than about the thing. The face belongs to the clock. At four in the afternoon it had no face at all, and arriving in the dark does not make it a truer picture. What the reversal does not say is that the daylight reading is correct and the night one is hysteria. It says a smaller room makes a bigger object. Nothing about the object changed.

meanings.altText: A full moon in line, with a single moth in front of it, above the numeral.

readingLines: Your Tuesday was good and there was nothing underneath it. No catch, nothing arriving later. A sunflower head on the plate, drawn face on. A good day with no subtext is not suspicious. It is just rarer than the other kind.
A sunflower head, face on, all of it visible at once. You had a good day this week and said so out loud. Naming it did not break it. Some warmth survives being said, and this was that kind.
You are waiting for the other half of it. There is no other half this time. That is a genuinely hard sentence to accept. A sunflower faces one direction and does not hedge. Tuesday was just good.
questions: Which day was it?
Who did you tell?
What are you waiting for?
meanings.libraryEntry: Some days are good all the way through and have nothing underneath them. No catch, no cost arriving on Thursday, no subtext at all. Those days are less common than the other kind, which is the only true thing suspicion has going for it, and they are not rare enough to justify the search. A sunflower head drawn face on is entirely visible at once and hedges in no direction. What this card is actually about is the reflex that follows a good day, which is to look for the price of it, and that reflex has a history, and is not paranoia, and protects nothing whatsoever. Warmth said out loud sometimes survives being said. That is the test the day passed. Nothing needs to be found. Your Tuesday passed that test. Nothing is owed on Thursday, and nothing is being held back until then.

readingLines: The good day happened and you let it be a good day. No inspection afterwards. No search for the cost. That restraint is harder than it sounds, and you managed it for a whole Tuesday. It counted.
You had a good day and spent the evening looking for the catch. Suspicion of the good is a habit with a history. It is not paranoia. It also protects nothing. The day was still good, and shorter.
You said the day was good and one person made it smaller. That happens. It is about them and their week. A sunflower does not close because the room disagreed. Tuesday stays on the record anyway.
questions: When did you let it stand?
What were you looking for?
Whose week was that about?
reversed.libraryEntry: Three things happen to a good day. In the first it is allowed to stand. No inspection afterwards, no hunt for the cost, and that restraint is considerably harder than it sounds and got managed for a whole Tuesday. In the second the evening goes to looking for the catch, which has a history behind it and is not paranoia, and which protects nothing, and the day ends up still good and several hours shorter. In the third it gets said out loud and somebody shrinks it. That is a fact about them and their week rather than about the day, and no flower has ever shut because a room disagreed with it. The day stays on the record. The record is not open to revision. You were there for it, which is the whole evidentiary basis, and it is enough for a Tuesday.

meanings.altText: A sunflower head seen face on, drawn in line, centered above the plate numeral.

readingLines: You read an old entry and recognised the handwriting and not the worry. Same hand. Different animal on the page. Whatever that was about, it resolved without you noticing the moment it stopped mattering. Most of them do.

A cicada shell, split down the back, the animal gone. You have outgrown a worry this year and did not attend the moment it happened. There was no announcement. The evidence is that you cannot get back into the old one.

Old journals are the only honest record of what you used to be afraid of. Memory edits. Paper does not. Reading your own handwriting about a worry that has since dissolved is the closest available look at your own scale.
questions: Which worry no longer reaches you?
What can you no longer feel?
Where were you a year ago?
meanings.libraryEntry: An old journal entry is the only unedited account of your former fears, because memory edits continuously and paper does not. The common experience of rereading one is a mild vertigo. The handwriting is yours and unmistakable, and the worry on the page belongs to a person you can no longer fully reach, and there was no moment at which it stopped mattering, or at least no moment you attended. A cicada shell splits down the back and the animal is elsewhere, and nothing about the shell records the hour it happened. What this card offers is scale, and scale is the least dramatic and most useful thing on the list. It is not a verdict on the earlier version of you, who had less to work with than you do. It is a measurement, taken twice, on a person who was moving the whole time.

readingLines: You read the entry and the worry had gone and you felt almost nothing about it. That flatness is the accurate response. Nothing to mark. A resolved thing does not owe you a feeling at the moment you notice it resolved.

You read the entry. The worry is still current, word for word, two years on. That is worth knowing plainly. Some shells do not split on schedule. A worry that has held the same size for two years is information. Not a verdict.
You reread the old entries in order to grade yourself. They are not a scorecard. The person who wrote them was working with what they had. Judgement in this card is a reading and not a sentence.
questions: What resolved without a ceremony?
Which one is still current?
Who were you grading?
reversed.libraryEntry: Two readings and a misuse. In the first, the worry has gone and you feel almost nothing about it, and the flatness is correct rather than cold, because a resolved thing owes you no feeling on the day you notice it has gone. Nothing needs marking. In the second, the entry reads as current two years on, down to the wording, and that is worth stating plainly rather than gently. Not every shell splits on schedule, and a worry that has not shrunk in two years is information rather than a verdict on you. The misuse is rereading in order to grade. Old entries are not a scorecard, and the person who filled them was working with the information available at the time, which was less than you have now. Judgement here is a reading taken twice on a person who kept moving between the two. It was never a sentence.

meanings.altText: An empty cicada shell split down the back, drawn in line above the plate numeral.

readingLines: The last box went out to the recycling on Sunday. The room took a year. A leaf wreath on the plate, closed, one continuous line. You are standing in finished. It has about four days before it becomes normal.
Completion has a short shelf life and no ceremony attached. A closed wreath, one line. No gap in it. You finished something this year that took the whole year. By Friday the room is just the room.

You are in the finished room and it feels slightly less than you expected. That is standard. It is not ingratitude. Endings are flatter than beginnings by a wide margin. You are allowed a minute in it.
questions: What did you just finish?
Where are you standing?
Bigger, or about this?
meanings.libraryEntry: The last box goes out to the recycling and the room is finished, a year after it started. What happens next is the actual subject of this card. Standing in a finished thing has a shelf life of roughly four days, after which the room is simply the room and the year it took is not visible in it at all. A leaf wreath is one continuous line with no gap, and a wreath with a gap is a stick. Completion arrives with no ceremony attached, because completions are not issued by anybody and no one else was counting the months. What tends to follow is a mild flatness, which reads as ingratitude and is not, since finishing is a much flatter event than starting and always has been. The minute you spend standing in it is the whole ritual on offer.

readingLines: You stood in the finished room for a minute before moving the sofa again. One minute is the whole ritual available. Endings do not get handed out. The wreath closes whether or not the join gets noticed.

Your last box is still in the hall and has been since March. Ninety-eight percent finished is a stable state. It is a comfortable one. A wreath with a gap in it is a stick. The gap is four inches wide.

You finished it and started the next room the same afternoon. Momentum is real. It is also a way of not standing anywhere. A closed wreath was closed for about ninety seconds. Then it was a floor plan.
questions: Who noticed the join?
Which box is still in the hall?
How long did finished last?
reversed.libraryEntry: Three things happen to a finished room. In the first it gets one minute. You stand in it before moving the sofa again, and that minute is the entire ritual available, because completions are not handed out and a ring closes on its own account, found or not. In the second there is one box left, in the hall, unopened since spring. Very nearly finished is a stable and comfortable state, and a ring left open is a stick, and the opening measures about four inches. In the third the following room begins before dinner. Momentum is genuine, and it is also a dependable method of never standing anywhere, and a closed wreath stayed closed for ninety seconds before becoming a floor plan. All three are ordinary. Only one of them includes the minute, and the minute is the part that is not available later.

meanings.altText: A closed ring of leaves drawn in one continuous line, centered above the numeral.

readingLines: First bud, out before the leaves. Nothing about it is defensible yet. You have an idea this week that arrived early, and early is what first looks like. It has no plan attached. Buds do not file plans.
You keep calling it premature. It is. That is the correct state for a thing this size, and prematurity is not a verdict on it. One bud on a bare branch, in weather that has not settled.

One sprig, budded, no leaves anywhere on the plate. Something started in you this week and you have already begun arguing it down. The arguing is premature too. No defence is required at this stage. The branch has weeks yet.
questions: What arrived early this week?
Who have you told, if anyone?
What would you do with it before lunch?
meanings.libraryEntry: Hawthorn buds before it leafs, which looks like a mistake and is a strategy. The bud is out in weather that could still turn, unprotected, weeks ahead of any support. Ideas arrive the same way. Formed enough to notice, nowhere near formed enough to defend, and the gap between those two states is where most of them get killed, usually by the person who had them. You do not owe anybody a case for something this new. That is the whole offer here. A first thing is allowed to be unreasonable, unfinished, and slightly embarrassing, and it stays viable for a surprisingly long time if it is simply recorded rather than argued about. What kills early is not weather. It is being asked to justify itself in February. February has never been a fair judge of anything green, and it is not one now.

readingLines: The bud opened and you wrote it down. That was the whole requirement. A recorded idea survives a bad month. An unrecorded one survives about four hours, and you have lost several that way already.

The idea got argued down before lunch. You did it yourself, thoroughly, and the case against was excellent. Cases against early things always are. There is nothing there yet to defend with. The branch is bare again.
Frost came. Or the enthusiasm did not last the week. Either way the bud is off the branch. Hawthorn buds again next year and is not diminished by this one. You have more first things than you think.
questions: Where did you write it down?
Who argued it down, exactly?
Frost, or just Thursday?
reversed.libraryEntry: Two failures and one success, and the success is almost too small to describe. You write the thing down. That is all. A recorded idea keeps for months in a notebook and costs nothing to keep, while an unrecorded one has a working life of about four hours, and you have lost several that way without noticing. The first failure is the internal prosecution. Early things get asked for their business case by the very person who had them, and they lose, because there is nothing there yet to argue with. That is not evidence against the idea. It is evidence about the timing of the question. The second failure is weather, plain and unremarkable. Some enthusiasms do not last the week and some frosts arrive in April. Hawthorn buds again the following year and treats the loss as ordinary, which it is.

meanings.altText: One budded hawthorn sprig, drawn large and centered, small ochre mark above.

readingLines: Two stakes, a field's width apart. You are holding two versions of next year and neither has been ruled out. That is a real position. Not indecision, and it has a time limit nobody has told you.
Two sprigs, evenly weighted, no third. Weighing is work and you have been doing it properly. The two is the hour before choosing, which is a legitimate place to stand and a poor place to live.
You can see both horizons from here. Neither is a mistake. What the two notices is only that the view is the same today as last month, and that a position held long enough stops being a position.
questions: Which horizon keeps coming back?
When does the choosing stop being free?
What has changed since last month?
meanings.libraryEntry: Two stakes on a plate, evenly weighted, with nothing between them. This is the deliberating card and deliberation gets an unfair reputation. Weighing two genuine prospects is real work, it takes real time, and rushing it produces worse outcomes than sitting with it does. Hawthorn is the suit of things set going, and even here nothing has moved yet. What the position costs is not visible at first. Two live options each require a small ongoing maintenance, a bit of attention held in reserve for a future that has not been chosen, and reserved attention is unavailable to you for anything else. Held for a week that is nothing. Held for a season it becomes the season. The tell is the view. If the horizons look exactly as they did last month, the weighing has finished without anybody announcing it, and what remains is not deliberation.

readingLines: One stake comes out. You picked, and the picking was not a revelation, it was Tuesday. The unchosen horizon stays on the map and stops asking for maintenance. That is most of what choosing buys.

You are still holding both, and now the holding is the plan. The two options have quietly become one arrangement, comfortable in a way neither option would be. Nobody chose this. It accumulated, one undecided week at a time.

One option expired while you weighed. Not punished, not lost through carelessness, just timed out, the way real prospects do. The remaining one is still good. It is simply the remaining one now. That is a different feeling.
questions: What did picking actually cost?
How long has the holding been the plan?
Which one timed out?
reversed.libraryEntry: Three endings and only one of them is a decision. In the first you choose, and the choosing turns out to be a Tuesday rather than a revelation, and the unchosen prospect stays on the map without asking for anything. The relief is disproportionate to the drama, which is the usual report. In the second the holding becomes the arrangement. Two live options settle into a comfortable third state that neither of them would have provided, and nobody selects that state, it accumulates one undecided week at a time until it is simply how things are. In the third, one option expires. Nothing was mishandled. Real prospects have real windows, they close on their own schedule, and afterward the remaining option is still perfectly good while feeling noticeably different, because being chosen and being left over are not the same thing.

meanings.altText: Two budded hawthorn sprigs, one above the other, small ochre mark above.

readingLines: You have refreshed the tracking page four times today. It has not moved. Three sprigs, planted, doing their own work now, and the sea does not consult the sender. Waiting is not a task, though it feels like one.

Three stakes on a ridge, looking out. You did the sending. What comes back is not yours to hurry, and the refreshing is a way of standing at the window that produces no weather. Ships arrive on their own schedule.

Something of yours is in transit and you cannot touch it. Three sprigs, spaced, patient. Early returns say something and not everything, and the part they do not say is the part you are refreshing for.
questions: What is genuinely in your hands today?
How many times did you check?
What are you refreshing for, exactly?
meanings.libraryEntry: Three sprigs on a ridge, spaced apart, all pointed the same way. The three is the watching card and it is the hardest of the early Hawthorns to sit inside, because everything about the suit's temperament wants to act and there is nothing left to act on. The sending happened. What returns is on somebody else's schedule and in somebody else's weather, and the refreshing you have been doing produces no wind. That is the honest mechanic. It is also worth separating two things that feel identical in the waiting. Some of your attention is genuinely needed, in case something arrives that requires an answer.
